questions.q: Per this lesson, every Salesforce access setting ultimately answers one of which two questions?
options: What can this user do, and which records can this user see
How much does this user cost, and how often do they log in
Which app is this user in, and which language do they use
How old is this user's account, and how many records do they own
questions.explain: The lesson splits every access question into object/field-level access (what a user can do) and record-level access (which records they can see).

questions.q: What controls object and field-level access ('what can this user do')?
options: Organization-wide defaults and the role hierarchy
Profiles, permission sets, and field-level security
Sharing rules and manual sharing
Public groups and queues
questions.explain: Profiles, permission sets, and field-level security answer the 'what can they do' question; OWD, roles, and sharing answer 'which records.'

questions.q: A user has full Edit access to the Account object but can't see a single Account record. What does this illustrate?
options: Object/field access and record-level access are independent, and both must pass
The user's profile is misconfigured and must be rebuilt
Object permissions automatically grant access to all records of that type
This situation is impossible in Salesforce
questions.explain: The lesson states explicitly that a user can have full object-level access and still see zero records, because the two systems are independent and both checks must pass.

questions.q: On the New User page in Setup, what do the Role and Profile fields illustrate about the security model?
options: They're redundant fields that do the same thing
They're optional fields admins can usually skip
They control record-level access and object/field-level access respectively — two different systems
Role controls object access and Profile controls record access
questions.explain: Profile governs what a user can do; Role governs which records open up to them through the hierarchy — the opposite pairing of the wrong answer.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say Salesforce layers multiple security mechanisms instead of using one all-powerful setting per user?
options: Layering is a legacy limitation Salesforce has not yet removed
A single per-user permission bit doesn't scale — layering keeps broad defaults cheap to maintain while still allowing precise exceptions
Each mechanism is sold as a separate product add-on
Layering exists only to make the admin certification exam harder
questions.explain: The lesson explains that layering lets Salesforce keep cheap, broad defaults while still supporting narrow exceptions without multiplying the baseline configuration.
